quote: I honestly, I just I would rather be off grid completely.
stewart_read: The customer is describing a fully off-grid intent (no utility connection at all, generator backup, battery, possible rainwater collection) which is a different product scenario than a standard grid-tied solar install. Ion's documented catalog doesn't clearly address off-grid systems, so it's unclear whether this is even a serviceable request — that judgment call is closer-tier, but the setter had an opportunity to flag the ambiguity rather than silently log it.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: rep should have asked a clarifying question or flagged this for the design team as a non-standard ask. Strategic read: since product-fit determination is explicitly closer-tier work per setter_scope_discipline, silently capturing the detail and letting the design team assess feasibility is defensible setter behavior.
coaching_implication: Flag for the closer: customer wants full utility disconnection, not a supplemental grid-tied system. This needs to be surfaced explicitly in the handoff, not just buried in notes, so the closer isn't caught flat-footed on a scenario Ion may or may not support.

quote: I do do I do just happen to have my most recent bill because you're not the only company I've been talking to, and the only way I could get it to them was to take a picture of it and send it to them via text message.
stewart_read: Customer explicitly discloses he's shopping multiple companies and has already sent his bill to at least one competitor, then later reveals a 65%-production shortfall from one of them. The rep never asks which company(ies) or what they proposed.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to ask a quick 'which companies have you talked to, and what did they show you?' — this is free competitive intel for the closer and takes seconds to capture.

quote: the problem they're having is they've only got 36 feet to run to work with.
stewart_read: This is the second touch on the competing-quote thread — the customer is now giving specific technical detail (run length, shading, winter solstice sun angle) about a competitor's proposed design. The rep listens and says 'Okay' without asking who provided this design or probing further.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: the rep's later response ('my team will explore all the options') is a correct scope-hold — she avoids debating the shading physics herself. But holding scope on the technical debate doesn't preclude a quick probe on which company gave him this design; those are separable moves and the second one was skipped.
coaching_implication: This is the second occurrence of the same missed-probe pattern — worth flagging as a pattern, not a one-off, in the 1-on-1.

quote: Yeah. My my team will we'll definitely explore all the options, see what we can do to get you, you know, as much production as possible, cover as much of your bill as you can.
stewart_read: Faced with a detailed technical objection about shading and winter-solstice sun angles, the rep correctly does not engage in a technical debate and instead bridges to the design team — a textbook universal_escape_hatch deflection, not scope creep.
coaching_implication: This is a positive example worth reinforcing: the rep held scope under a customer who clearly has technical fluency and could have pulled her into a debate she wasn't equipped to win.

quote: There is an option for a TPO. My credit's good enough that I could finance it myself, but I would also have to take out a loan.
stewart_read: Customer raises financing structure (TPO vs. self-financing) unprompted — a signal he's already thinking concretely about how to pay for this. The rep's response ('I will fill my keys in' / moving to wrap-up) files it without reflecting it back as something the appointment will resolve.
coaching_implication: A quick 'that's exactly the kind of option my specialist will walk through with you tomorrow' would have tied this detail forward into the appointment rather than letting it sit as an unaddressed aside.

quote: not just me. Laura and I, my wife.
stewart_read: The customer names his wife as part of the household decision context seconds after confirming no one else is on the title. This isn't a spouse_decision protocol trigger (no decision-gate language like 'I need to talk to her'), but it is a co-decider awareness signal the rep never follows up on to confirm whether Laura should be included on the appointment.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: rep should have asked if Laura wants to be on the design call. Strategic read: since Ronald didn't frame her as a required decision-maker or gatekeeper, the rep's choice not to interrupt verify flow to probe further is a minor, low-stakes omission rather than a protocol violation.
coaching_implication: Light-touch coaching: when a spouse is named, a quick 'would she want to join the design call too?' costs nothing and protects the appointment from a later 'I need to check with my wife' surprise at close.

quote: Well, my psychiatrist worries about it, but
stewart_read: Customer discloses a mental-health detail (seeing a psychiatrist) in the context of the self-defense/wildlife conversation. The rep's response is a bare 'Man.' with no acknowledgment or bridge.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: this disclosure came inside off-topic rapport banter (deer, AR-15, wildlife) rather than a moment of vulnerability tied to solar decision-making, so a heavier response may have felt intrusive or off-script. Reactive read: any vulnerability disclosure is a trust gift per schema and deserves more than a one-word filler.
coaching_implication: Not a call-costing moment, but worth naming: a slightly warmer acknowledgment ('sounds like you've got a lot going on') costs nothing and keeps the human connection intact without turning it into a therapy conversation.
